Within this third edition of the AMD catalog, an AMD network system is defined as follows: An AMD network system represents a system of multiple AV fleet applications across the spectrum of vehicle sizes and types; operating within a geographically defined district; providing fully automated, on-demand, and fixed-schedule transport services; and fully integrated with regional high-capacity transit service, existing manual modes serving the district, and the various forms of pedestrian and micromobility activity within the district. To further define various on-demand services that will be common in an AMD network system, two additional terms will be used throughout this third edition as “operating modes”: 9 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. • Real-time, on-demand dispatch mode: Mobility services that respond without an advance reservation but rather provide a demand response of the system for an immediate pickup of the passenger as soon as possible. • Scheduled, on-demand dispatch mode: Mobility services that are scheduled in advance with a prescribed time for pickup of the passenger. Through the advancement of AV technology, public transit agencies may ultimately be able to cost-effectively operate fleets of the smallest vehicle sizes to provide private rides for single travel parties that fully complement and integrate with the fleets of larger transit vehicles providing shared-ride passenger service for longer regional access. It is acknowledged, however, that the implementation of an AMD network system, particularly in the near term, will be a blend of transport services operating both automatically and under human control. 2.5 Example of a Large-Scale AMD Network System When fully integrated, the blended types of AV transport services described previously will be capable of providing highly optimized internal circulation within the district and FMLM connections to regional transit stations within or nearby the district. Figure 1 and Figure 2, which illustrate fully automated transport services within a major urban district, were taken from a 2019 study for Houston, Texas (Lott 2019). The concept was developed independently of NLR research but is synonymous with the NLR AMD concept. Within the context of Houston, regional transit is served by an extensive network of high-occupancy vehicle (HOV) lanes within the Houston freeway medians—an existing busway system that stretches throughout the metropolitan area. This regional bus system is a prospective application of automated bus operations.
